title: Malachi 2:10–17
context: The prophet asks why the people deal treacherously with one another when they share one Father and Creator (2:10). Judah has married the daughter of a foreign god (2:11–12), and the people weep at the altar when the LORD refuses their offerings. They ask, “Why?”, and the LORD answers that he is witness between a man and “the wife of your youth,” whom he has betrayed (2:13–15). In 2:16 the WEB reads, “One who hates and divorces … covers his garment with violence!”; other translations render the verse differently, for example as the LORD saying he hates divorce, and the Hebrew is difficult. The unit closes with another disputation: the people have wearied the LORD by asking, “Where is the God of justice?” (2:17), a question chapter 3 answers.

verses.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?” Arminian readers see covenant brotherhood violated by unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s shared Creator and covenant as the ground for faithfulness to one another. Shared ground: treachery against a brother is treachery against the covenant of the fathers.

verses.text: Judah has dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah has profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god.
verses.arminianNotes: “Judah has dealt treacherously,” and “has married the daughter of a foreign god.” Arminian readers see marriage to worshipers of other gods as covenant unfaithfulness, as in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the concern as religious faithfulness rather than ethnicity, since the issue is “a foreign god.” Readers in this tradition read the verse alongside Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13, cited by reference.

verses.text: The LORD will cut off the man who does this, him who wakes and him who answers, out of the tents of Jacob and him who offers an offering to the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD will cut off the man who does this,” “out of the tents of Jacob.” Arminian readers see a serious warning against covenant betrayal, even for those who still bring offerings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the gravity of the offense. The phrase “him who wakes and him who answers” is obscure, and readers in this tradition hold its precise meaning with caution.

verses.text: “This again you do: you cover the LORD’s altar with tears, with weeping, and with sighing, because he doesn’t regard the offering any more, neither receives it with good will at your hand.
verses.arminianNotes: “you cover the LORD’s altar with tears,” “because he doesn’t regard the offering any more.” Arminian readers see worshipers grieving that God rejects their offerings while ignoring the reason.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see emotional worship that does not address the sin behind God’s displeasure. Readers in this tradition note that the following verse supplies the reason the people ask for.

verses.text: Yet you say, ‘Why?’ Because the LORD has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion and the wife of your covenant.
verses.arminianNotes: The people ask, “Why?” The LORD answers that he “has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously.” Arminian readers see marriage as a covenant God witnesses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see marriage as “the wife of your covenant,” a bond before God. Shared ground: faithlessness to a spouse is treated as a sin against the LORD himself, read pastorally and with sober care.

verses.text: Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought godly offspring. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.
verses.arminianNotes: “Did he not make you one,” “He sought godly offspring.” Arminian readers commonly hear an echo of Genesis 2:24, though the Hebrew of this verse is notoriously difficult.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the creation pattern of one flesh behind the verse, cited by reference to Genesis 2:24. The wording is difficult, and readers in this tradition hold detailed interpretations with care.

verses.text: One who hates and divorces”, says the LORD, the God of Israel, “covers his garment with violence!” says the LORD of Armies. “Therefore pay attention to your spirit, that you don’t be unfaithful.
verses.arminianNotes: “One who hates and divorces”, says the LORD, “covers his garment with violence!” Arminian readers see the LORD condemning treacherous divorce as a kind of violence against the wronged spouse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s strong opposition to faithless divorce. Translations render the verse differently, and readers in this tradition hold the precise wording with care while affirming the call to faithfulness.

verses.text: You have wearied the LORD with your words. Yet you say, ‘How have we wearied him?’ In that you say, ‘Everyone who does evil is good in the LORD’s sight, and he delights in them;’ or ‘Where is the God of justice?’
verses.arminianNotes: “You have wearied the LORD with your words.” The people ask, “How have we wearied him?” and say, “Where is the God of justice?” Arminian readers see cynicism about God’s justice exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people questioning whether God cares about justice. Shared ground: the question sets up the LORD’s answer in chapter 3, where he promises to come to his temple in judgment (3:1, 5).
